canonical_question: Could the 'high dislocation density' contribute to the 'superior mechanical properties' mentioned in the title, and is this effect retained at high temperatures?

question_variants.question: Could the 'high dislocation density' contribute to the 'superior mechanical properties' mentioned in the title, and is this effect retained at high temperatures?
question_variants.resolution_summary: High dislocation density is explicitly cited as a contributor to outstanding mechanical properties at both low and high temperatures. The text confirms this mechanism holds up at high temperatures (700°C or higher).

answers.answer: High dislocation density contributes to the superior mechanical properties. The text states that outstanding properties at high temperatures (700°C or higher) are achieved with high dislocation density and fine precipitates.
answers.measurement_outcome: Outstanding mechanical properties at high temperatures attributed to high dislocation density
answers.mechanism: Dislocation density and fine precipitates strengthen the material
evidence_spans: SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution.
In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides.

Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present.

source_evidence_spans: The SLM-built HEA has a higher dislocation density of 1.88 × 10 14 m −2 as compared to the homogenized HEA [33] .
